title: Image recognition based on optical spike processing with exciton-polaritons
authors: Olgierd Jeziorski, Jakub Rogala, Krzysztof Tyszka
abstract: Exciton-polariton condensates combine ultrafast dynamics with strong optical nonlinearities, making them promising for optical neuromorphic computing. Here, we numerically demonstrate image recognition using the transient response of an exciton-polariton condensate. Downscaled MNIST images are encoded as optical pulse sequences, and the resulting condensate dynamics are sampled and processed by a linear classifier. For ten-class classification, condensate features achieve 92.2% accuracy, compared with 91.4% for raw-pixel linear classification. Combining both feature sets increases the accuracy to 93.2%. For the challenging binary classification of digits 7 and 9, the combined model reaches 97.3%, exceeding both the linear (95.5%) and feed-forward neural-network (96.6%) baselines. These results demonstrate that polariton dynamics can extract useful nonlinear features for ultrafast optical information processing.
summary: This study demonstrates the use of exciton-polariton condensates as a platform for optical neuromorphic computing, achieving image recognition on MNIST. By encoding images into the temporal dynamics of the condensate, the system extracts nonlinear features that significantly boost classification accuracy when combined with raw pixel data. This confirms the potential of polariton dynamics for ultrafast optical information processing.
main_problem: The paper addresses the need for fully optical, energy-efficient, and fast neuromorphic computing systems capable of performing image recognition.
main_result: By encoding MNIST images into optical pulse sequences, the exciton-polariton condensate dynamics achieved 93.2% accuracy when combining condensate features with raw pixel data, outperforming linear baselines.
method: The MNIST dataset is encoded into a time-domain pump function $P(t)$, and the resulting nonlinear dynamics of the condensate are sampled and processed by a linear classifier.
model_or_system: The physical system is an exciton-polariton condensate governed by coupled ODEs describing condensate, active reservoir, and inactive reservoir populations. The dynamics are analyzed across optimal, under-stimulated, and saturated regimes.
key_observables: Classification accuracy (e.g., 92.2% baseline, 93.2% combined), condensate density $n_C(t)$, and the temporal evolution of the system variables.
important_parameters: Optimal operating parameters include $\Delta t \approx 30 	ext{ ps}$ and pulse width $\approx 5 	ext{ ps}$. The analysis distinguishes between optimal, under-stimulated, and saturated regimes.
main_assumptions: The analysis uses a single-mode approximation, neglecting spatial variations, and relies on mapping pixel intensities to time-domain pump pulses.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the dynamics in different operational regimes (optimal vs. under-stimulated) and compare classification accuracy across four models (raw pixels, pure condensate, combined, FFN) against varying sampling resolutions ($N$).
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the physical model and the encoding of image data into temporal pulses. It then analyzes the system's performance across different operational regimes, demonstrating the nonlinear feature extraction capability, and concludes with quantitative comparisons of classification accuracy.
why_interesting: This work directly applies nonlinear, many-body physics (exciton-polaritons) to a machine learning task, demonstrating how inherent nonlinear dynamics can act as a feature extractor, which is highly relevant to open quantum systems and nonlinear optics.
